blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Articles 233 to 237 in Part VI of the Constitution regulate the organization and functioning of subordinate courts in India.
District Judges are appointed, posted, and promoted by the Governor of the State in consultation with the High Court (Article 233).
Recruitment of persons other than district judges to the judicial service is conducted by the Governor in consultation with the State Public Service Commission and the High Court (Article 234).
The High Court exercises complete administrative control over district courts and subordinate courts, including postings, promotions, and leave (Article 235).
The subordinate judiciary comprises Civil Courts, Criminal Courts (Sessions Court), Revenue Courts, Family Courts, and alternative dispute mechanisms like Lok Adalats.

blocks.content: Subordinate Courts form the lowest tier of the Indian judicial system. They work below the High Courts and deal with the majority of cases in the country.
These courts are called 'Subordinate Courts' because they function under the control and supervision of the High Courts.
They play a very important role because common people directly interact with these courts for justice.
CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS RELATED TO SUBORDINATE COURTS
The provisions related to Subordinate Courts are mentioned in Part VI of the Indian Constitution (Articles 233 to 237).

Article 235 – Control of High Court over Subordinate Courts

blocks.content: Subordinate Courts are courts which are subordinate to the High Court. They include:

items:
• District Courts
  • Sessions Courts
  • Civil Courts
  • Criminal Courts
  • Revenue Courts
  • Family Courts
  • Lok Adalats (under Legal Services Authorities Act)
Lok Adalats (under Legal Services Authorities Act)

blocks.content: The hierarchy of courts in a State is as follows:
District Court is the highest court at the district level.
The District Court is the highest judicial authority in a district. It deals with:

items:
• Civil cases (as District Judge)
  • Criminal cases (as Sessions Judge)

blocks.content: The District Judge is the head of all subordinate courts in the district.
District Judges are appointed by the Governor of the State in consultation with:

• Must be an advocate or pleader for at least 7 years
  • Recommended by the High Court

High Court exercises complete control over subordinate courts. This includes:

items:
• Posting and promotion of judges
  • Granting leave
  • Disciplinary action
  • Supervision of work

blocks.content: Civil Courts deal with civil disputes such as:

items:
• Property disputes
  • Marriage and divorce cases
  • Contract disputes
  • Succession cases

blocks.content: Criminal Courts deal with criminal cases and offences. Hierarchy:

items:
• Sessions Judge
  • Additional Sessions Judge
  • Chief Judicial Magistrate
  • Judicial Magistrate First Class
  • Judicial Magistrate Second Class

items:

They aim at speedy and peaceful settlement.
Lok Adalats are established under Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. They aim to:

items:
• Provide free legal aid
  • Settle disputes amicably
  • Reduce burden on courts

blocks.content: Decisions of Lok Adalat are binding and final.

items:
• Control of High Court
  • Security of service
  • Fixed service conditions
  • Protection from executive interference
Appointment of District Judges is made by the Governor in consultation with the High Court, NOT the State Public Service Commission.
Administrative control over subordinate courts rests entirely with the High Court under Article 235, maintaining judicial independence.
A Sessions Judge has the authority to award capital punishment (death sentence), but it must be confirmed by the High Court before execution.
Lok Adalats are statutory bodies under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, whose awards are final and binding with no provision for appeal.

blocks.content: Subordinate Courts are the backbone of the Indian judicial system.
They directly serve the people and ensure justice at the grassroots level. Strengthening subordinate courts is essential for speedy justice and strong democracy.
